content.intro: Tiling a bathroom, kitchen backsplash, entryway, or shower creates a stylish, moisture-resistant surface that endures daily wear for decades. Because cutting perimeter tiles, corner joints, and pipe penetrations always produces fractured pieces, accurate material planning with a proper waste buffer prevents project stoppages. This free tile calculator computes the total square footage of your surface and determines both the individual tile count and required carton quantities based on your selected tile dimensions. Enter your installation dimensions below to calculate exact materials, order from identical manufacturing dye lots, and achieve clean, professional grout lines.
content.howItWorks: Total installation area is calculated by multiplying length in feet by width (or wall height) in feet. The surface area of an individual tile is determined by multiplying tile length by width in inches and dividing by 144 (for example, a 12 × 12 inch tile equals 1.0 square foot; a 6 × 6 inch tile equals 0.25 square feet). The surface area is adjusted by the waste allowance (typically 10% for straight grid patterns or 15% for diagonal herringbone layouts) and divided by individual tile area. Dividing the total tile count by the number of tiles per box and rounding up gives the required box quantity.

examples.title: A 10 by 8 foot bathroom floor with 12 by 12 inch tiles
examples.text: For a bathroom floor measuring 10 × 8 feet, the surface area is 80 square feet. Each 12 × 12 inch tile covers exactly 1.0 square foot. Adding a 10% cutting waste allowance: 80 × 1.10 = 88 tiles. At 10 tiles per retail carton, 88 ÷ 10 = 8.8, which rounds up to 9 boxes.

examples.title: A 12 by 10 foot kitchen floor with 12 by 24 inch large format tiles
examples.text: For an area measuring 120 square feet using 12 × 24 inch tiles (2.0 sq ft per tile) with a 15% waste factor for offset staggered placement: 120 × 1.15 = 138 square feet. Total tiles needed: 138 ÷ 2.0 = 69 tiles. At 8 tiles per carton: 69 ÷ 8 = 8.625, requiring 9 boxes.

commonMistakes: Ordering without an extra 10% to 15% waste allowance, resulting in running out of tiles near the finish line.
Mixing tile boxes with different dye lot numbers, leading to subtle shade and tone mismatches under lighting.
Failing to account for tile thickness and grout joint width when planning subfloor and door transitions.
Using non-modified thinset mortar instead of polymer-modified thinset for large format porcelain tiles.

faq.q: Why is a 10% to 15% waste allowance recommended for tile?
faq.a: Cutting tiles along perimeter walls, around toilet flanges, plumbing pipes, and corners creates offcuts that frequently cannot be used elsewhere. A 10% buffer is recommended for straight square layouts, while diagonal, herringbone, or chevron patterns require 15% due to extensive angle cutting.

faq.q: How does grout joint width affect tile calculations?
faq.a: Grout joints (typically 1/16 to 1/4 inch) slightly expand the coverage of each tile. However, because tile dimensions are nominal rather than exact, professional installers treat grout joint width as a safety margin rather than subtracting it from the tile count.

faq.q: What is a tile dye lot, and why does it matter?
faq.a: A dye lot refers to a specific production batch fired together in the kiln. Even slight temperature or humidity variations alter the glaze color and tile dimensions between batches. Always verify that all boxes share the identical dye lot number on their packaging.

faq.q: Should I keep spare tiles after the project is finished?
faq.a: Yes. Keep at least half a box to a full box of spare tiles. If a tile cracks due to subfloor movement or you replace a fixture in the future, matching discontinued tiles years later is nearly impossible.
